## Conclusion

Cities with severe, persistent central-area congestion and a transit network able to absorb diverted trips should adopt it; cities without both should not, and the question as posed hides that split. The implemented schemes reduced traffic volumes and delays and raised substantial net revenue, and none of the three reviewed here has been repealed [1][2][3]. The strongest objection is distributional — a flat cordon charge takes a larger share of income from poorer drivers than richer ones — and it is not a reason to reject pricing so much as a constraint on design: the incidence depends on who drives, what the alternatives are, and where the revenue goes [4][5]. Adopt, in other words, is conditional on the transit alternative and on the revenue rule, and a scheme that fails either is worse than no scheme.

## Key findings

- London's 2003 charge reduced traffic in the zone by roughly 15 percent in its first year and cut delays by about 30 percent [1].
- Stockholm's 2006 trial reduced zone traffic by around 20 percent, and a referendum held after the trial converted it into a permanent scheme [2].
- New York's 2025 scheme reduced average daily vehicle entries to the Manhattan central business district by 13 percent in March relative to the historical March average [3].
- The incidence of a cordon charge is not uniformly regressive: it depends on car ownership by income, on the alternatives available, and above all on how the revenue is spent [4][5].
- In the Stockholm case, the charge's direct burden was mildly regressive before revenue use was accounted for, and the sign of the net effect turned on what the revenue funded [4].

## The strongest counterargument

The objection that has killed schemes politically is distributional, and it is a good one. A cordon charge is a flat fee: two drivers pay the same to cross, and the one earning less pays a larger share of income. Where lower-income workers hold the jobs with hours transit does not serve — early shifts, night shifts, trips that chain childcare onto commuting — the charge falls hardest on the drivers least able to switch. Eliasson and Mattsson find the direct burden of the Stockholm charge mildly regressive before revenue use is considered [4], and that is the version of the objection to answer, not a weaker one about motorists in general.

What the objection gets right is that the direct burden is real and that "the revenue funds transit" is a promise, not a mechanism. Where it is incomplete is that incidence is an empirical question rather than a property of pricing as such: Santos and Rojey show the sign of the distributional effect varies with the city's geography, with who owns cars, and with the alternatives available, and can be progressive in cities where poorer residents are less likely to drive into the priced area [5]. The conclusion above is tempered rather than overturned by this: adoption is conditioned on a transit alternative and on a binding revenue rule, and a city that cannot supply both should expect the objection to hold in its case.

## Evidence from implementations

London's 2003 charge reduced traffic in the zone by roughly 15 percent in its first year and cut delays by about 30 percent, effects that persisted through the monitoring period [1]. Stockholm's 2006 trial reduced zone traffic by around 20 percent; the referendum that followed converted the trial into a permanent scheme, and support was substantially higher after residents had experienced it than before [2].

The MTA's first-quarter monitoring covers the January 5 start through March 31 rather than reporting one quarter-wide percentage. By March, average daily vehicle entries to the Manhattan central business district were 13 percent below the historical March average [3]. The scheme is too new in that report for longer-run effects to be read from it.

## Design and revenue

Scheme design matters more than the decision to price. Cordon schemes are simpler to administer but create sharp boundary effects at the cordon edge, where drivers reroute to avoid the charge and push traffic onto adjacent streets [2]. Corridor and distance-based schemes avoid that but require denser sensing infrastructure.

Revenue use is the lever that decides the distributional question rather than a footnote to it. Both the London and Stockholm schemes direct net revenue to transit capital programmes [1][2], and Eliasson and Mattsson's Stockholm analysis finds that where the revenue goes can outweigh the direct burden of the charge in the net incidence calculation [4].
